canonical_summary: The complete 2026 guide to FCC satellite licensing: 47 CFR Part 25 as it stands, the 25.122 small satellite track with its exact eligibility numbers, GSO queue and NGSO processing rounds, milestone and surety bond math, current application and regulatory fees, the 5-year deorbit rule, market access for non-US operators, and the adopted-but-not-yet-codified Part 100 overhaul of July 2026.
h1: FCC satellite licensing in 2026: the complete guide
meta_title: FCC satellite licensing 2026: Part 25, small sats, Part 100
meta_description: How FCC satellite licensing works in 2026: Form 312 and Schedule S, the 47 CFR 25.122 small sat track, fees, bonds, milestones, the 5-year deorbit rule, and the adopted Part 100 overhaul. Every number cited to the eCFR.
tldr: Commercial satellites are licensed under 47 CFR Part 25: file FCC Form 312 with Schedule S electronically in ICFS, pay $2,555 (small satellite track) to $17,670 (NGSO system) in application fees, and expect roughly 6 to 9 months for a straightforward small sat grant. Qualifying small satellites (10 or fewer, under 180 kg, 6-year orbital lifetime) skip processing rounds entirely. Satellites launched after September 29, 2024 must deorbit within 5 years of end of mission. On July 22, 2026 the FCC adopted a new Part 100 to replace Part 25, but those rules are not yet codified, so Part 25 remains governing law during the transition. Invariant prepares and ships these filings for space teams: agents draft Form 312 and Schedule S with every answer traced to its source rule, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the application through grant.

sections.heading: Which FCC regime covers your mission
paragraphs: Any satellite that transmits or receives radio signals under US jurisdiction needs FCC authorization, and the FCC runs three distinct regimes. Commercial service is licensed under 47 CFR Part 25, issued under the Communications Satellite Act of 1962 and the Communications Act of 1934. Experimentation, product development, and market trials fall under Part 5, the Experimental Radio Service, which is how most university and first-time technology demonstration missions fly. Amateur radio satellites operate under Part 97. The regimes differ in cost, speed, and what you are allowed to do with the spacecraft: a Part 5 license cannot support commercial service, and a Part 25 license is overkill for a one-off technology demo.
One rule now spans all three regimes: the 5-year post-mission deorbit requirement applies to Part 25, Part 5, and Part 97 satellites alike, and to non-US satellites granted US market access.

sections.heading: August 2026 status: Part 25 governs, Part 100 is coming
paragraphs: On July 22, 2026 the FCC adopted a Report and Order and Further Notice (FCC 26-47, SB Docket 25-306) that discards Part 25 and rebuilds satellite licensing from first principles as a new Part 100. The Commission describes the target state as a licensing assembly line: modularized applications, bright-line public interest criteria, revised license terms, surety bonds, and processing rounds, mandatory space situational awareness data sharing, and a further rulemaking on a space-based experimental regime. Law firm summaries note default license terms extending from 15 to 20 years and the elimination of surety bonds for GSO operators and NGSO systems licensed outside processing rounds.

None of that is codified yet. As of the August 1, 2026 eCFR snapshot, Title 47 contains no Part 100 and Part 25 remains the governing rule set. Applications filed today are Part 25 applications. The practical posture for an operator: file under Part 25 as written, and track the transition, because bond obligations and processing mechanics will change under your feet. Everything below states current law.

sections.heading: The application: Form 312, Schedule S, and ICFS
paragraphs: A space station application is a comprehensive proposal filed on FCC Form 312: the Main Form carries the applicant's legal, ownership, and qualification information, and Schedule S carries the structured technical data required by 47 CFR 25.114(c): orbital parameters and planes, frequency bands, power flux density levels, beam contours, and estimated operational lifetime, plus the narrative exhibits of 25.114(d), including the orbital debris mitigation showing. Filing is electronic only, through the International Communications Filing System (ICFS); the Commission will not accept paper, and the application fee is due at filing.

GSO applicants can file in two steps under 25.110(b)(3): a draft ITU coordination request with a simplified Form 312 first, then the full application within two years. Before filing anything, tell the Space Bureau you are coming: the FCC's published guidance recommends contacting satinfo@fcc.gov, engaging more than six months ahead for atypical missions, and filing 6 to 8 months before launch for small satellite missions.

sections.heading: The small satellite track: 47 CFR 25.122
paragraphs: The streamlined track is the best deal in the rulebook if you qualify. It carries a $2,555 application fee instead of $17,670, skips processing rounds entirely under 25.157(i), gives the Space Bureau a cleaner review (the FCC's own FAQ describes roughly 6 to 9 months for straightforward, uncontested applications), and relaxes the surety bond deadline to one year plus 30 days after grant. The tradeoff is a 6-year license term with no extension and no replacement authorization.
Eligibility is certification against hard numbers. The main criteria under 25.122:
bullets: 10 or fewer space stations per application, NGSO only
Mass of 180 kg or less per satellite, including propellant
At least 10 cm in the smallest dimension
Total in-orbit lifetime of 6 years or less per satellite
Deployment at or below 600 km, or propulsion with collision avoidance and deorbit capability
Collision probability with large objects of 0.001 or less over the orbital lifetime
Disposal by atmospheric reentry with zero calculated casualty probability and success probability of at least 0.9
Unique telemetry marker and ground-commandable transmission cessation
No operational debris, and loss-of-control probability from small debris of 0.01 or less

sections.heading: Standard track: queues, rounds, milestones, and bonds
paragraphs: Standard Part 25 licenses run 15 years. GSO applications sit in a first-come, first-served queue under 25.158 and are considered in filing order. NGSO applications go through processing rounds under 25.157: a lead application on public notice opens a round with a cut-off date, competing systems file into it, every qualified applicant is granted, and if spectrum is insufficient it is divided equally among the licensees.

Grants come with a clock and a bond. Under 25.164, a GSO licensee must launch and operate within 5 years; an NGSO licensee must have 50 percent of the authorized constellation up and operating within 6 years and the full system within 9. Under 25.165, a surety bond must be posted within 30 days of grant or the license is null and void automatically, a trap that has killed real licenses. The bond escalates with time: NGSO from $1 million toward $5 million over about six years, GSO from $1 million toward $3 million over about five. Surrendering a license before a milestone, or missing one, is a default and the Treasury collects.

sections.heading: What it costs in 2026
paragraphs: Two separate bills. Application fees, from the current 47 CFR 1.1107 fee table: $4,175 per GSO satellite, $17,670 per NGSO system, $2,555 for a small satellite or small spacecraft application, $2,930 for a modification, $1,685 for special temporary authority, and $425 for a typical transmit-receive earth station.

Then annual regulatory fees, which dwarf the application fees for commercial systems. The FY2025 schedule (FCC 25-52): $141,790 per authorized GSO station, $375,140 per NGSO system under 1,000 authorized satellites, $1,917,390 per NGSO system at 1,000 or more, $12,330 per small satellite license, and $2,060 per earth station authorization. Since FY2025 the fee attaches to authorized stations at the start of the fiscal year, operational or not. Operators whose total liability is $1,000 or less are exempt.

sections.heading: The 5-year deorbit rule
paragraphs: Adopted September 29, 2022 in FCC 22-74, the first binding deorbit rule: space stations ending their mission in or passing through low Earth orbit below 2,000 km, disposing by uncontrolled atmospheric reentry, must complete disposal as soon as practicable and no later than 5 years after end of mission. End of mission means the point where the spacecraft can no longer maneuver to avoid collisions. The rule reaches FCC licensees, small sats, experimental and amateur satellites, and non-US operators with US market access.

Grandfathering is now mostly exhausted: satellites already in orbit in 2022 are exempt, but the two-year grace period ended, and satellites launched after September 29, 2024 must comply. The codified companion numbers in 25.114(d)(14) still apply: disposal success probability of at least 0.9, reentry casualty risk below 1 in 10,000, and large-object collision probability below 0.001. Waivers exist for good cause but the Commission has said they will not be liberally granted, with academic and research missions getting a distinct waiver analysis.

sections.heading: How long it takes
paragraphs: The FCC has bound itself to deadlines at the front of the pipeline: since January 2024 the Space Bureau must act on acceptability within 30 days for earth station and GSO applications and 60 days for NGSO applications, either putting the application on public notice or telling the applicant what is wrong. Once on public notice, there is a 30-day comment window under 25.151(d), plus a 15-day reply period when comments come in.

End to end, the honest numbers: roughly 6 to 9 months for a straightforward, uncontested small satellite application per the FCC's own FAQ, and 12 to 24 months or more for complex commercial systems, with waiver requests, federal shared spectrum bands requiring NTIA coordination, novel operations, contested filings, and processing rounds as the recognized delay drivers. Plan the license like a critical-path item, not paperwork: for a small sat, the FCC recommends filing 6 to 8 months before launch.

sections.heading: Non-US operators: market access under 25.137
paragraphs: A satellite licensed by another administration reaches the US market through a petition for declaratory ruling, filed in ICFS with the same legal and technical showing Part 25 demands of a US licensee, Schedule S included. Fees mirror the license fees: $4,175 GSO, $17,670 NGSO, $2,555 small satellite. Non-US NGSO systems join processing rounds and non-US GSO systems enter the queue once the system is operating, licensed elsewhere, or submitted for ITU coordination. Market access grantees carry the same milestones, the 25.165 bond if the system is not yet in orbit, US regulatory fees, and the 5-year deorbit rule. An ECO-Sat competitive showing applies only to non-WTO-member licensing administrations.

sections.heading: How applications die
paragraphs: Most failed applications are not denied, they are dismissed. Under 25.112 the Bureau returns applications that are defective for incomplete answers, missing informational showings, or internal inconsistencies, that fail to substantially comply with the rules without a waiver request, or that duplicate a pending application in a queue or round. Failure to respond to Bureau correspondence on time is dismissal for failure to prosecute, with prejudice if the application is mutually exclusive with another.

The two deadliest traps sit outside the application itself: the surety bond that must arrive within 30 days of grant on the standard track, and ITU cost-recovery fees, where an overdue invoice without a pending appeal dismisses every application associated with that satellite network under 25.111(d). Internal consistency is the quiet killer across all of it: Schedule S, the debris showing, the ITU filing, and any NOAA or export control representations describe one spacecraft, and reviewers cross-read them.

sections.heading: The licenses the FCC does not issue
paragraphs: The FCC authorizes the radio system. A real mission usually needs more. Earth-imaging capability triggers a NOAA remote sensing license under 15 CFR Part 960, with its own 60-day determination clock. International spectrum rights run through ITU coordination, with the FCC as the US notifying administration and a signed declaration accepting ITU cost recovery filed in ICFS under 25.111. Ground infrastructure needs its own earth station licenses. The launch itself is the launch provider's FAA license under 14 CFR Part 450, with its statutory 180-day review clock. Export control sits over everything: most satellite hardware and technical data are ITAR or EAR controlled regardless of what the FCC grants.

This is the coordination problem that makes satellite licensing expensive in practice: five workstreams, five agencies, one spacecraft, and every filing must stay consistent with the others as the design evolves. faqs.question: How do I get an FCC license for a satellite?
faqs.answer: File FCC Form 312 with Schedule S electronically through the FCC's International Communications Filing System (ICFS), with the application fee paid at filing. The application must be a comprehensive proposal under 47 CFR 25.114, including orbital parameters, frequency plans, and an orbital debris mitigation showing. The FCC recommends contacting the Space Bureau at satinfo@fcc.gov before filing, and filing 6 to 8 months before launch for small satellite missions.

faqs.question: How much does an FCC satellite license cost?
faqs.answer: Application fees under the current 47 CFR 1.1107 table: $2,555 for a qualifying small satellite application, $4,175 per GSO satellite, and $17,670 for an NGSO system. Annual regulatory fees are far larger for commercial systems: in FY2025, $141,790 per GSO station, $375,140 per NGSO system under 1,000 satellites, $1,917,390 for 1,000 or more, and $12,330 per small satellite license.

faqs.question: How long does FCC satellite licensing take?
faqs.answer: Roughly 6 to 9 months for a straightforward, uncontested small satellite application, per the FCC's published FAQ, and 12 to 24 months or more for complex commercial systems. The Space Bureau must complete its acceptability review within 30 days for GSO and earth station applications and 60 days for NGSO applications, followed by a 30-day public notice comment period. Waivers, federal shared bands, novel operations, and processing rounds are the main delay drivers.

faqs.question: What qualifies as a small satellite under FCC rules?
faqs.answer: Under 47 CFR 25.122: 10 or fewer NGSO satellites per application, each 180 kg or less including propellant, at least 10 cm in the smallest dimension, with a total in-orbit lifetime of 6 years or less, deployed at or below 600 km or carrying propulsion, with large-object collision probability of 0.001 or less, disposal by atmospheric reentry with zero calculated casualty risk, a unique telemetry marker, and commandable transmission cessation. The license term is 6 years with no extension.

faqs.question: What is FCC Part 100?
faqs.answer: Part 100 is the new satellite licensing framework the FCC adopted on July 22, 2026 in FCC 26-47 to replace Part 25: a licensing assembly line with modular applications, bright-line public interest criteria, revised bonds, terms, and processing rounds, and mandatory space situational awareness data sharing. As of August 2026 it is adopted but not yet codified in Title 47, so Part 25 remains the governing rule set during the transition.

faqs.question: What is the FCC 5-year deorbit rule?
faqs.answer: Adopted September 29, 2022 in FCC 22-74: satellites ending their mission in or passing through LEO below 2,000 km and disposing by uncontrolled atmospheric reentry must complete disposal no later than 5 years after end of mission. It applies to FCC-licensed satellites, experimental and amateur satellites, and non-US satellites with US market access. Satellites launched after September 29, 2024 must comply; those already in orbit in 2022 are exempt.

faqs.question: What is the FCC surety bond for satellite licenses?
faqs.answer: Under 47 CFR 25.165, standard-track licensees must post a surety bond within 30 days of grant or the license is automatically null and void. The bond escalates from $1 million toward $5 million for NGSO systems over about six years, and from $1 million toward $3 million for GSO over about five. Small satellite licensees get one year plus 30 days. Missing a milestone or surrendering the license early is a default paid to the US Treasury.

faqs.question: Do foreign satellite operators need FCC approval?
faqs.answer: To serve the US market, yes. A non-US-licensed operator files a petition for declaratory ruling under 47 CFR 25.137 with the same technical showing required of US licensees, pays the same application fees, joins the same GSO queue or NGSO processing rounds, and carries US regulatory fees, milestone obligations, the surety bond if not yet operating, and the 5-year deorbit rule.

faqs.question: Why do FCC satellite applications get dismissed?
faqs.answer: Under 47 CFR 25.112: defective or internally inconsistent applications, failure to substantially comply with the rules without a waiver request, duplicates of pending applications, and failure to respond to Bureau correspondence on time. Outside the application, the two big traps are missing the 30-day surety bond deadline, which voids the license automatically, and overdue ITU cost-recovery fees, which dismiss every application tied to that satellite network.

faqs.question: Who can prepare and file an FCC satellite application for us?
faqs.answer: No FCC rule requires the application to come from an attorney: the applicant files its own Form 312 and Schedule S through ICFS. Operators use space law firms, spectrum consultants, or a licensing platform. Invariant runs the full pipeline: agents draft the application with every answer traced to the rule that requires it, keep it consistent with the ITU, NOAA, and export control workstreams, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the filing through grant, including regulator correspondence.

faqs.question: Does a satellite operator need licenses besides the FCC's?
faqs.answer: Usually. Earth imaging requires a NOAA remote sensing license under 15 CFR Part 960. International spectrum protection requires ITU coordination filed through the FCC. Ground stations need their own earth station licenses. The launch runs on the launch provider's FAA Part 450 license. And satellite hardware and technical data are typically ITAR or EAR controlled, which governs every cross-border exchange regardless of FCC status.
